newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Iran Central Bank says no plans to devalue rial.
newsitem.headline: Iran Central Bank says no plans to devalue rial.

text.p: Iran's Central Bank said on Sunday it does not plan to devalue the rial currency.

Central Bank Governor General Mohsen Nourbakhsh "stated that the foreign exchange situation of the country is such that there is no need to increase the rates," the official Iranian news agency IRNA reported.

Iran banned free currency exchange in May 1995, setting an official rate of 3,000 rials to the dollar following a drop to 7,000 rials to the dollar when Washington imposed unilateral trade and investment sanctions against Tehran.
The rial remained steady on the illegal black market when Washington imposed a new set of sanctions against Iran in July.
It is currently trading at 4,200 rials to the dollar.

IRNA said Nourbakhsh "rejected rumours on increase in foreign exchange rates," adding that "sufficient hard currency needed for different sectors including industry, investment and purchase of essential goods have been provided."
Iran's economy has been suffering since the 1979 Islamic revolution, with a drop in oil revenue and huge costs of the 1980-88 war with Iraq.

Earlier on Sunday the daily Iran newspaper quoted the head of the state Plan and Budget Organisation, Hamid Mirzadeh, as saying that Tehran's hard currency revenue mainly from crude oil exports was expected to exceed budget forecast by $2 billion in the current Iranian year which started on March 20.
Oil revenue is Iran's main hard currency earner and the government's major source of financing if it is to meet debts which officials have put at almost $22 billion.
The budget for the current Iranian year envisages petroleum earnings of $15.99 billion, based on exports of 2.6 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude and a weighted average barrel price of $15.50.
OPEC member Iran is the world's third largest oil exporter with a daily quota of 3.6 million barrels.
